title: IEEE VIS Publications: Growth, Venue Mix, and the Journal Turn
subtitle: A guided-to-open exploration of how 3,877 IEEE VIS papers changed from 1990 through 2024.
overview: The IEEE VIS record is not just a story of more papers; it is a story of changing containers for those papers. The surprising endpoint is 2024, when journal papers account for 100.0% of 124 papers. The stem first separates annual volume from venue concentration, then shows that the deeper structural change is the move from conference-paper dominance toward journal-paper dominance. The bowl lets readers test that turn against collaboration size, keyword coverage, and paper-type leadership years.

takeaway: The panels converge on one conclusion: IEEE VIS changed less by simple expansion than by rebalancing into a journal-centered publication record, with Vis remaining the largest venue grouping and collaboration/metadata measures maturing by 2024. What follows is practical: read any long-run VIS trend through paper type and venue mix before attributing it to overall community growth. The conclusion would change if later years returned to a conference-paper majority or if the 2024 journal-only endpoint proved to be a normalization artifact.
stem_title: From paper volume to publication structure
stem_note: Read the first four panels in order: they move from the count of papers, to the venue producing the most papers, to yearly venue mix, and finally to the paper-type shift. Together they build the case that composition, not just volume, explains the modern record.
bowl_note: Use the remaining panels to test whether the journal turn aligns with collaboration, keyword coverage, and the years when each paper kind leads.
